blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Managing warehouse operations well means combining physical organisation with a steady operational rhythm. A clean layout and a well-trained team are only half the battle; the other half is daily discipline: cycle counts every day, picking errors tracked and addressed, damaged goods investigated the same week, forklifts maintained on schedule, safety drills taken seriously.

Warehouses reward routine more than they reward heroics. The best ones look almost boring: the same checks, the same meetings, the same small corrections, done the same way every day. The ones that drift into 'we'll sort it later' habits slowly accumulate silent problems that reveal themselves, all at once, at the worst possible moment.

A good warehouse manager is the least dramatic person in the building — and quietly, by a wide margin, the most effective.

items.q: According to the text, a clean layout and a well-trained team are…
options: all that a good warehouse needs
items.why: "A clean layout and a well-trained team are only half the battle" — a outra metade é a disciplina diária.

items.q: What does the text say the best warehouses look like?
options: Almost boring, with the same checks every day
items.why: "The best ones look almost boring: the same checks, the same meetings… every day."

items.q: What happens to warehouses that drift into 'we'll sort it later' habits?
options: They save time in the short term
They accumulate silent problems that appear all at once
They reduce their need for cycle counts
items.why: "slowly accumulate silent problems that reveal themselves, all at once, at the worst possible moment."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Routine tends to prevent problems rather than create them.
Small corrections done consistently add up over time.
Daily discipline matters as much as good organisation.
A dramatic, firefighting manager is a sign of a well-run warehouse.
items.why: Inferência: o texto elogia o gestor "least dramatic" — o herói que apaga incêndios é o oposto do ideal.

items.q: The final line suggests that effectiveness in a warehouse comes mainly from…
options: reacting quickly when things go wrong
quiet, consistent routine rather than spectacle
items.why: Inferência: "the least dramatic person… quietly… the most effective" liga eficácia à constância silenciosa, não ao drama.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Emily orientando o novo supervisor de armazém. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let's be honest about what you've walked into. Your predecessor ran this place on adrenaline — brilliant on a bad day, useless on a normal one. So before we talk about anything clever, we're going to build a rhythm.

Start with the morning walk-through. It must happen before a single order is processed — no exceptions, even when you're short-staffed. You check the aisles, the forklifts, the safety notices, and yesterday's picking errors. Ten minutes, every day.

Then the receiving bays. Every bay has to be cleared by ten. That's not my preference, that's the site rule, and the audit checks it. If a bay is still full at eleven, something upstream is already broken, and you want to know that early, not at five o'clock.

One more thing. You need to know your team's real capacity before you hand out tasks. Don't guess. If you promise more than the floor can carry, the errors and the injuries follow, and then everyone calls it a people problem. It isn't. Chaos in a warehouse is always a leadership problem.

Build the routine first. Trust me — once the routine holds, the exceptions almost take care of themselves.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: How does Emily describe the previous supervisor?
options: Focused only on the receiving bays
Brilliant on a bad day, useless on a normal one
items.why: "Your predecessor ran this place on adrenaline — brilliant on a bad day, useless on a normal one."

items.q: When must the morning walk-through happen?
options: After the receiving bays are cleared
At the end of each shift
Only when the team is short-staffed
Before a single order is processed
items.why: "It must happen before a single order is processed — no exceptions."

items.q: Why does Emily want every receiving bay cleared by ten?
options: Because forklifts are only available before ten
Because the team leaves at ten
Because it is the site rule and the audit checks it
items.why: "That's not my preference, that's the site rule, and the audit checks it."

items.q: What does Emily imply if a bay is still full at eleven?
options: The team simply needs to work faster
A problem further up the process has already started
The bay should be ignored until five o'clock
items.why: Inferência: "something upstream is already broken" — a bandeja cheia é sintoma de um problema anterior no fluxo.

items.q: What is Emily's underlying message about chaos in the warehouse?
options: It reflects leadership, not the people on the floor
It is caused by weak or careless staff
It is normal and cannot be prevented
It only happens when the warehouse is understaffed
items.why: Inferência: ela rejeita o rótulo de "people problem" — "Chaos in a warehouse is always a leadership problem."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "We reorganised the layout so pickers walk shorter routes." A layout is…
options: the physical arrangement of the space
items.why: Layout = disposição, o arranjo físico do espaço.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "We run a ___ every morning to check stock levels without stopping the whole warehouse."
items.why: Cycle count = contagem cíclica, feita em partes do estoque todos os dias.

items.q: "Three orders went out with the wrong items — a classic picking error." A picking error is…
options: a mistake made when selecting items for an order
items.why: Picking error = erro de separação, quando se coleta o item errado para o pedido.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "The pallet fell during unloading, so we logged it as ___ and pulled it from stock."
items.why: Damaged goods = mercadoria avariada, retirada do estoque.

items.q: "We hold a monthly safety drill so everyone knows the exits." A safety drill is…
options: a practice exercise to prepare for emergencies
items.why: Safety drill = simulado de segurança, um exercício de prática para emergências.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem na gestão de um armazém. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The site manager still has to sign off on the new shift plan." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We'll roll out the new cycle-count routine aisle by aisle." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva.

items.q: "Two supervisors pushed back on the ten-o'clock deadline." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "The team agreed to track errors daily but never followed through." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "If a bay is still full, deal with it early — don't sort it out at five o'clock." To sort it out means to…
items.why: Sort it out = resolver, dar um jeito no problema.
